title: Jev in Practice: A Composable Python Toolkit for TypeSafe's System One Decision Model
description: Jev is TypeSafe's flagship System One decision model: instead of generating text, it answers typed questions (Choice, Score, Noul) about a state with calibrated probabilities that software can branch on directly. This work presents daf-jev, an open, modular, composable Python toolkit for the Jev API, together with a live-API characterization of the model. The package layers ergonomic question builders, a decision-composition library (confidence gates, tiered routing, composite scoring), a concurrent corpus evaluator, a calibration module, a CLI, an agent skill, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server over a thin typed client. Live benchmarks show that batching questions into one call is faster and cheaper than sequential calls (up to ~18x speedup and ~4x fewer tokens), that decision pipelines complete within the model's millisecond envelope, and that reported confidence is self-consistent across repeated evaluations. All numbers in the accompanying manuscript are generated from benchmark artifacts; the full provenance chain (hashed documentation snapshot, figure registry, validation receipts) is machine-checked.
release_name: v0.6.0 — Jev as a factor source for graphical models

methods.name: daf-jev layered Python client for the System One endpoint
methods.description: Implements typed builders (noul, choice, score), sync/async clients with a pure retry policy, and a typed exception hierarchy over one HTTP endpoint.
methods.evidence: daf-jev is organized as a strict layering: an ergonomic surface (CLI, MCP server, scripts, benchmarks) on top of pure-logic composition, on top of primitives and wire types, on top of a single transport and client layer that owns all I/O.

methods.name: Pure-function decision patterns and a concurrent batch Evaluator
methods.description: composite_score, confidence_gate, and route/pick turn typed answers into decisions locally; the Evaluator runs a fixed question set over many states without aborting on failures.
methods.evidence: Per-state failures never abort the batch; they are captured into the evaluation record alongside the answers and the measured latency, so one malformed state cannot cost the run.

methods.name: Live-API batching benchmark at batch widths 5, 10, and 20
methods.description: Compares one batched call against sequential single-question calls on the jev-latest model, recording wall time and token totals.
methods.evidence: The batching benchmark compares two strategies over the same state and question mix: one call carrying all questions in a batch, versus one sequential single-question call per question, repeated for each configured batch width over multiple measured runs.

methods.name: Self-consistency calibration benchmark (6 states × 5 repeats)
methods.description: Scores choice answers against the modal choice across repeats and noul answers by pairwise stability, computing ECE and Brier score without external ground truth.
methods.evidence: benchmarks/bench_calibration.py runs 6 short states 5 times each against the jev-latest model and scores choice answers under a self-consistency proxy

methods.name: No-mock test suite and hash-manifested documentation snapshot
methods.description: Unit tests drive the real transport against a local HTTP server; model claims are grounded in a 108-page hashed snapshot of the vendor documentation.
methods.evidence: The test suite follows the no-mock convention: unit tests drive the real transport against a real local HTTP server fixture, and live tests hit the real API only when a key is present in the environment

key_findings: Batching questions into one call gave wall-time speedups of 3.98, 8.77, and 18.55 across the configured batch widths.
At the widest batch width the sequential strategy used 4.22 times the tokens of the batched call, so batching was both faster and cheaper.
End-to-end decision pipelines had median wall times of 0.133 s (composite scoring) and 0.129 s (intent routing).
Under a self-consistency proxy, the calibration benchmark reported ECE 0.0730 and Brier 0.0252; the author notes this shows consistency with proxy labels, not correctness about the world.
The unit test suite reached 93.08 measured coverage.
key_findings_evidence: Batching a batch’s worth of questions into one call yields wall-time speedups of 3.98, 8.77, and 18.55 across the configured batch widths
the sequential strategy consumes 4.22 times the tokens of the batched call at the widest setting — batching is simultaneously faster and cheaper.
End-to-end decision pipelines complete at a median wall time of 0.133 for composite scoring and 0.129 for intent routing, so confidence-gated decisions can sit inline on interactive request paths.
The expected calibration error of 0.0730 and the Brier score of 0.0252 indicate that reported choice confidence is broadly consistent with the proxy labels
The unit test suite stands at 93.08 measured coverage

summary_provenance.method: Evidence-grounded extraction from full_text.md: every method and finding carries a verbatim quote from the paper text, mechanically verified to occur in full_text.md (whitespace/ligature-normalized) before merge.
summary_provenance.notes: All benchmarks are single-model (jev-latest) live-API measurements from one session (2026-09-16); the paper flags live-API variance, early-access documentation, and the self-referential calibration proxy as limitations.
